title: Die zwei Brüder
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 60. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng/giengen, fieng, hieng, Thüre, Thiere, thun/thust, gethan, todt, ward und gerieth).
about: By far the longest tale in the collection (KHM 60), and really several strung end to end: the golden bird whose heart and liver make gold, the dragon-slayer robbed of his victory, and the twin who takes his brother’s place and lays a sword down the middle of the marriage bed. Its length is part of the pleasure — the beasts are gathered one by one, the errands to the king’s table are told out one by one, and nothing is hurried. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, and in the wager scene the huntsman addresses the innkeeper in the third person (“sieht er, Herr Wirth”), an old courtesy for which English has nothing but a plain “you.”

sentences.t: Es waren einmal zwei Brüder, ein reicher und ein armer.
sentences.l: There were once two brothers, a rich one and a poor one.

sentences.t: Der reiche war ein Goldschmied und bös von Herzen: der arme nährte sich davon, daß er Besen band, und war gut und redlich.
sentences.l: The rich one was a goldsmith and evil of heart: the poor one nourished himself from this, that he bound brooms, and was good and honest.
sentences.i: The rich one was a goldsmith, and evil at heart; the poor one made his living by binding brooms, and was good and honest.
sentences.n: “sich nähren davon, daß …” — literally “to feed oneself from the fact that …,” that is, to make one’s living by doing something. redlich is an old-fashioned word for honest and upright.

sentences.t: Der arme hatte zwei Kinder, das waren Zwillingsbrüder und sich so ähnlich wie ein Tropfen Wasser dem andern.
sentences.l: The poor one had two children, they were twin brothers and so alike to one another as one drop of water to the other.
sentences.i: The poor man had two children, twin brothers, as like each other as one drop of water is to another.
sentences.n: ähnlich takes a dative object: one drop is like “dem andern,” to the other.

sentences.t: Die zwei Knaben giengen in des reichen Haus ab und zu, und erhielten von dem Abfall manchmal etwas zu essen.
sentences.l: The two boys went to and fro in the rich one’s house, and received from the leavings sometimes something to eat.
sentences.i: The two boys came and went in the rich brother’s house, and now and then got something to eat from the scraps.
sentences.n: “ab und zu gehen” is used here in its older, concrete sense — to go in and out, to come and go; on its own “ab und zu” has since narrowed to “now and then.” “des reichen Haus” puts the genitive before its noun, a placement Grimm uses freely.

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß der arme Mann, als er in den Wald gieng Reisig zu holen, einen Vogel sah, der ganz golden war und so schön, wie ihm noch niemals einer vor Augen gekommen war.
sentences.l: It came to pass that the poor man, as he went into the forest to fetch brushwood, saw a bird which was entirely golden and so beautiful as never yet one had come before his eyes.
sentences.i: It came to pass that the poor man, going into the forest to gather brushwood, saw a bird that was all of gold, and more beautiful than any that had ever come before his eyes.
sentences.n: “einem vor Augen kommen” — to come before someone’s eyes, that is, to be laid eyes on.

sentences.t: Da hob er ein Steinchen auf, warf nach ihm und traf ihn auch glücklich: es fiel aber nur eine goldene Feder herab und der Vogel flog fort.
sentences.l: Then he picked a little-stone up, threw at it and hit it too luckily: there fell however only a golden feather down and the bird flew away.
sentences.i: So he picked up a pebble, threw it at the bird, and by good luck hit it; but only a golden feather fell down, and the bird flew off.
sentences.n: “nach etwas werfen” = to throw at something. glücklich here means “luckily,” not “happily.”

sentences.t: Der Mann nahm die Feder und brachte sie seinem Bruder, der sah sie an, und sprach „es ist eitel Gold,“ und gab ihm viel Geld dafür.
sentences.l: The man took the feather and brought it to his brother; that one looked at it and said “it is sheer gold,” and gave him much money for it.
sentences.i: The man took the feather and brought it to his brother, who looked at it and said, “It is pure gold,” and gave him a great deal of money for it.
sentences.n: eitel here carries its old adverbial sense, “nothing but, sheer” — “eitel Gold” is solid gold, not vain gold.

sentences.t: Am andern Tag stieg der Mann auf einen Birkenbaum und wollte ein paar Äste abhauen: da flog derselbe Vogel heraus, und als der Mann nachsuchte, fand er ein Nest, und ein Ei lag darin, das war von Gold.
sentences.l: On the other day the man climbed up a birch-tree and wanted to hew off a couple of branches: then flew the same bird out, and when the man searched, he found a nest, and an egg lay in it, that was of gold.
sentences.i: The next day the man climbed a birch tree, meaning to cut off a few branches; out flew that same bird, and when the man searched he found a nest with an egg lying in it, and the egg was of gold.

sentences.t: Er nahm das Ei mit heim und brachte es seinem Bruder, der sprach wiederum, „es ist eitel Gold,“ und gab ihm was es werth war.
sentences.l: He took the egg home with him and brought it to his brother, who said again, “it is sheer gold,” and gave him what it was worth.

sentences.t: Zuletzt sagte der Goldschmied „den Vogel selber möcht ich wohl haben.“
sentences.l: At last the goldsmith said “the bird itself I should like well to have.”
sentences.i: At last the goldsmith said, “I should very much like to have the bird itself.”
sentences.n: möcht (for möchte) softened by wohl is a wish half-admitted: “I should rather like.” The object stands first for weight.

sentences.t: Der Arme gieng zum drittenmal in den Wald und sah den Goldvogel wieder auf dem Baum sitzen: da nahm er einen Stein und warf ihn herunter und brachte ihn seinem Bruder, der gab ihm einen großen Haufen Gold dafür.
sentences.l: The poor one went for the third time into the forest and saw the gold-bird sitting on the tree again: then he took a stone and threw it down and brought it to his brother, who gave him a great heap of gold for it.
sentences.i: The poor man went into the forest a third time and saw the golden bird sitting in the tree again; so he took a stone and brought it down, and carried it to his brother, who gave him a great heap of gold for it.
sentences.n: “warf ihn herunter” — the ihn is the bird, brought down by the stone; German lets the two masculine objects share a pronoun and trusts the sense.

sentences.t: „Nun kann ich mir forthelfen“ dachte er und gieng zufrieden nach Haus.
sentences.l: “Now I can help myself onward,” thought he, and went contented toward home.
sentences.i: “Now I can get by,” he thought, and went home content.
sentences.n: “sich forthelfen” = to help oneself along, to manage, to make shift.

sentences.t: Der Goldschmied war klug und listig, und wußte wohl was das für ein Vogel war.
sentences.l: The goldsmith was clever and cunning, and knew well what kind of a bird that was.

sentences.t: Er rief seine Frau, und sprach „brat mir den Goldvogel und sorge daß nichts davon weg kommt: ich habe Lust ihn ganz allein zu essen.“
sentences.l: He called his wife and said “roast me the gold-bird and see to it that nothing of it comes away: I have a mind to eat it entirely alone.”
sentences.i: He called his wife and said, “Roast me the golden bird, and see that nothing of it goes missing; I have a mind to eat it all by myself.”
sentences.n: “Lust haben zu …” = to feel like doing something; sorgen with a daß-clause is “see to it that.”

sentences.t: Der Vogel war aber kein gewöhnlicher, sondern so wunderbarer Art, daß wer Herz und Leber von ihm aß, jeden Morgen ein Goldstück unter seinem Kopfkissen fand.
sentences.l: The bird was however no ordinary one, but rather of so wondrous a kind that whoever ate heart and liver of it found every morning a gold-piece under his pillow.
sentences.i: But the bird was no ordinary one; it was of so wondrous a kind that whoever ate its heart and liver found a gold piece under his pillow every morning.
sentences.n: A creature whose heart and liver pass its virtue to whoever eats them is an old and widespread motif; the tale takes it as known. “so wunderbarer Art” is a genitive of quality, “of such a wondrous kind.”

sentences.t: Die Frau machte den Vogel zurecht, steckte ihn an einen Spieß und ließ ihn braten.
sentences.l: The woman made the bird ready, stuck it on a spit and let it roast.
sentences.i: The wife dressed the bird, put it on a spit and set it roasting.
sentences.n: “zurecht machen” = to prepare, to get ready — here to dress a bird for the fire.

sentences.t: Nun geschah es, daß während er am Feuer stand, und die Frau anderer Arbeiten wegen nothwendig aus der Küche gehen mußte, die zwei Kinder des armen Besenbinders hereinliefen, sich vor den Spieß stellten und ihn ein paarmal herumdrehten.
sentences.l: Now it happened that while it stood at the fire, and the woman on account of other work necessarily had to go out of the kitchen, the two children of the poor broom-binder ran in, placed themselves before the spit and turned it round a couple of times.
sentences.i: Now it happened that while it stood at the fire, and the wife was obliged to leave the kitchen on other business, the poor broom-binder’s two children ran in, planted themselves in front of the spit and turned it round a few times.
sentences.n: “anderer Arbeiten wegen” places wegen after its genitive noun — older and more formal than modern “wegen anderer Arbeiten.”

sentences.t: Und als da gerade zwei Stücklein aus dem Vogel in die Pfanne herabfielen, sprach der eine „die paar Bischen wollen wir essen, ich bin so hungrig, es wirds ja niemand daran merken.“
sentences.l: And as just then two little-pieces fell down out of the bird into the pan, the one said “these few little-bits we will eat, I am so hungry, no one will notice it thereby.”
sentences.i: And just then two little pieces fell out of the bird into the pan, and one of them said, “Let us eat these few scraps; I am so hungry, and nobody will ever be the wiser.”
sentences.n: Bischen is the 1857 spelling of bißchen. “an etwas merken” is to tell something *from* a thing — nobody will be able to tell from the bird that anything is gone; wirds = wird es.

sentences.t: Da aßen sie beide die Stückchen auf; die Frau kam aber dazu, sah daß sie etwas aßen und sprach „was habt ihr gegessen?“
sentences.l: Then they both ate the little-pieces up; the woman came however upon it, saw that they were eating something and said “what have you eaten?”
sentences.i: So the two of them ate the pieces up; but the wife came upon them, saw that they were eating something, and said, “What have you eaten?”
sentences.n: “dazu kommen” = to come upon a thing while it is going on.

sentences.t: „Ein paar Stückchen, die aus dem Vogel herausgefallen sind,“ antworteten sie.
sentences.l: “A couple of little pieces that have fallen out of the bird,” they answered.

sentences.t: „Das ist Herz und Leber gewesen,“ sprach die Frau ganz erschrocken, und damit ihr Mann nichts vermißte und nicht böse ward, schlachtete sie geschwind ein Hähnchen, nahm Herz und Leber heraus und legte es zu dem Goldvogel.
sentences.l: “That has been heart and liver,” said the woman quite terrified, and so that her husband should miss nothing and not grow angry, she quickly slaughtered a little-cock, took heart and liver out and laid it with the gold-bird.
sentences.i: “That was the heart and the liver,” said the wife, thoroughly frightened; and so that her husband should miss nothing and not fly into a rage, she quickly killed a young cockerel, took out its heart and liver, and laid them with the golden bird.
sentences.n: ward is the older past of werden (modern wurde); it runs through the whole tale.

sentences.t: Als er gahr war, trug sie ihn dem Goldschmied auf, der ihn ganz allein verzehrte und nichts übrig ließ.
sentences.l: When it was done, she served it up to the goldsmith, who consumed it entirely alone and left nothing over.
sentences.i: When it was done, she served it up to the goldsmith, who devoured the whole of it alone and left nothing.
sentences.n: gahr is the 1857 spelling of gar, said of meat cooked through. auftragen = to serve up a dish.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen aber, als er unter sein Kopfkissen griff, und dachte das Goldstück hervor zu holen, war so wenig wie sonst eins zu finden.
sentences.l: The next morning however, when he reached under his pillow and thought to fetch the gold-piece forth, there was as little a one to be found as at other times.
sentences.i: But the next morning, when he reached under his pillow and expected to draw out the gold piece, there was no more there than on any other day.
sentences.n: “so wenig wie sonst” — as little as at any other time, which is to say none at all. The clause is impersonal (“war … zu finden”), which English turns into “there was … to be found.”

sentences.t: Die beiden Kinder aber wußten nicht was ihnen für ein Glück zu Theil geworden war.
sentences.l: The two children however did not know what a fortune had fallen to their share.
sentences.i: But the two children had no idea what good fortune had come to them.
sentences.n: “zu Theil werden” (modern zuteil werden) = to fall to someone’s lot. “was ihnen für ein Glück” splits “was für ein” around the rest of the clause.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen, wie sie aufstanden, fiel etwas auf die Erde und klingelte, und als sie es aufhoben, da warens zwei Goldstücke.
sentences.l: The next morning, as they got up, something fell onto the ground and rang, and when they picked it up, there they were two gold-pieces.
sentences.i: The next morning, as they got up, something fell on the ground with a ring; and when they picked it up, it was two gold pieces.
sentences.n: warens = waren es.

sentences.t: Sie brachten sie ihrem Vater, der wunderte sich und sprach „wie sollte das zugegangen sein?“
sentences.l: They brought them to their father, who wondered and said “how should that have come about?”
sentences.i: They brought them to their father, who marvelled and said, “How can that have come about?”
sentences.n: zugehen, said of events, = to happen, to come about; it returns later as “wie soll das zugehen?”

sentences.t: Als sie aber am andern Morgen wieder zwei fanden, und so jeden Tag, da gieng er zu seinem Bruder und erzählte ihm die seltsame Geschichte.
sentences.l: But when they found two again the next morning, and so every day, then he went to his brother and told him the strange story.

sentences.t: Der Goldschmied merkte gleich wie es gekommen war und daß die Kinder Herz und Leber von dem Goldvogel gegessen hatten, und um sich zu rächen und weil er neidisch und hartherzig war, sprach er zu dem Vater „deine Kinder sind mit dem Bösen im Spiel, nimm das Gold nicht, und dulde sie nicht länger in deinem Haus, denn er hat Macht über sie und kann dich selbst noch ins Verderben bringen.“
sentences.l: The goldsmith noticed at once how it had come about and that the children had eaten heart and liver of the gold-bird, and in order to revenge himself and because he was envious and hard-hearted, he said to the father “your children are in play with the Evil One, do not take the gold, and suffer them no longer in your house, for he has power over them and can yet bring you yourself into ruin.”
sentences.i: The goldsmith saw at once how it had happened, and that the children had eaten the golden bird’s heart and liver; and to revenge himself — for he was envious and hard-hearted — he said to the father, “Your children are in league with the Evil One. Do not take the gold, and do not suffer them in your house any longer, for he has power over them, and may bring you to ruin as well.”
sentences.n: “der Böse” is the Evil One, the devil; “mit dem Bösen im Spiel sein” is to be mixed up with him. “ins Verderben bringen” = to bring to ruin.

sentences.t: Der Vater fürchtete den Bösen, und so schwer es ihm ankam, führte er doch die Zwillinge hinaus in den Wald und verließ sie da mit traurigem Herzen.
sentences.l: The father feared the Evil One, and hard as it came to him, he yet led the twins out into the forest and left them there with a sorrowful heart.
sentences.i: The father feared the Evil One; and hard as it went with him, he led the twins out into the forest all the same, and left them there with a heavy heart.
sentences.n: “es kam ihm schwer an” — impersonal ankommen, “it came hard to him,” that is, it cost him dearly.

sentences.t: Nun liefen die zwei Kinder im Wald umher und suchten den Weg nach Haus, konnten ihn aber nicht finden, sondern verirrten sich immer weiter.
sentences.l: Now the two children ran about in the forest and sought the way home, but could not find it, and instead strayed ever further.
sentences.i: Now the two children ran about the forest looking for the way home, but they could not find it, and only strayed further and further.

sentences.t: Endlich begegneten sie einem Jäger, der fragte „wem gehört ihr Kinder?“
sentences.l: At last they met a huntsman, who asked “to whom do you belong, children?”
sentences.i: At last they came upon a huntsman, who asked, “Whose children are you?”
sentences.n: “wem gehört ihr” — literally “to whom do you belong”: the old way of asking what family a child comes from.

sentences.t: „Wir sind des armen Besenbinders Jungen“ antworteten sie und erzählten ihm daß ihr Vater sie nicht länger im Hause hätte behalten wollen, weil alle Morgen ein Goldstück unter ihrem Kopfkissen läge.
sentences.l: “We are the poor broom-binder’s boys,” they answered, and told him that their father had not wanted to keep them in the house any longer, because every morning a gold-piece lay under their pillow.
sentences.i: “We are the poor broom-binder’s boys,” they answered, and told him that their father had not wanted to keep them in the house any longer, because every morning a gold piece lay under their pillow.
sentences.n: hätte … behalten wollen and läge are subjunctives of reported speech: the huntsman is being told this, and the tale keeps its distance from it.

sentences.t: „Nun,“ sagte der Jäger, „das ist gerade nichts schlimmes, wenn ihr nur rechtschaffen dabei bleibt und euch nicht auf die faule Haut legt.“
sentences.l: “Well,” said the huntsman, “that is just nothing bad, if you only stay honest along with it and do not lay yourselves on the lazy hide.”
sentences.i: “Well,” said the huntsman, “there is no great harm in that, so long as you stay honest about it and do not lie about idle.”
sentences.n: “sich auf die faule Haut legen” — to lay oneself down on the lazy hide, that is, to idle away one’s time.

sentences.t: Der gute Mann, weil ihm die Kinder gefielen und er selbst keine hatte, so nahm er sie mit nach Haus und sprach „ich will euer Vater sein und euch groß ziehen.“
sentences.l: The good man, because the children pleased him and he himself had none, so he took them home with him and said “I will be your father and raise you up.”
sentences.i: The good man, since the children pleased him and he had none of his own, took them home with him and said, “I will be your father and bring you up.”
sentences.n: The subject is named first and then resumed by “so nahm er” — a spoken construction the tales keep. “groß ziehen” = to rear, to bring up.

sentences.t: Sie lernten da bei ihm die Jägerei, und das Goldstück das ein jeder beim Aufstehen fand, das hob er ihnen auf, wenn sies in Zukunft nöthig hätten.
sentences.l: They learned there with him the huntsman’s craft, and the gold-piece that each one found on getting up, that he laid up for them, in case they should need it in future.
sentences.i: There they learned the huntsman’s craft from him; and the gold piece that each of them found on rising he laid by for them, against a time when they might need it.
sentences.n: aufheben here = to keep, to put by. hätten is subjunctive — a need not yet real.

sentences.t: Als sie herangewachsen waren, nahm sie ihr Pflegevater eines Tages mit in den Wald und sprach „heute sollt ihr euern Probeschuß thun, damit ich euch frei sprechen und zu Jägern machen kann.“
sentences.l: When they had grown up, their foster-father took them one day with him into the forest and said “to-day you shall do your trial-shot, so that I can speak you free and make you into huntsmen.”
sentences.i: When they had grown up, their foster father took them with him into the forest one day and said, “Today you shall make your trial shot, so that I can release you from your apprenticeship and make huntsmen of you.”
sentences.n: Probeschuß and freisprechen come from the world of the guilds: an apprentice was “spoken free” — released from his indentures — once he had produced his proof-piece, and for a huntsman that piece is a shot.

sentences.t: Sie giengen mit ihm auf den Anstand und warteten lange, aber es kam kein Wild.
sentences.l: They went with him to the stand and waited long, but no game came.
sentences.n: der Anstand is the hunter’s standing-place, the spot where he waits for game to pass.

sentences.t: Der Jäger sah über sich und sah eine Kette von Schneegänsen in der Gestalt eines Dreiecks fliegen, da sagte er zu dem einen „nun schieß von jeder Ecke eine herab.“
sentences.l: The huntsman looked above himself and saw a chain of snow-geese flying in the shape of a triangle, then he said to the one “now shoot one down from each corner.”
sentences.i: The huntsman looked up and saw a skein of snow-geese flying in the shape of a triangle, and said to the one of them, “Now bring one down from each corner.”
sentences.n: Kette is the hunting word for a line of birds flying together; English says a skein of geese.

sentences.t: Der thats und vollbrachte damit seinen Probeschuß.
sentences.l: That one did it and accomplished with it his trial-shot.
sentences.i: He did it, and so accomplished his trial shot.
sentences.n: thats = that es (modern tat es).

sentences.t: Bald darauf kam noch eine Kette angeflogen und hatte die Gestalt der Ziffer Zwei: da hieß der Jäger den andern gleichfalls von jeder Ecke eine herunterholen, und dem gelang sein Probeschuß auch.
sentences.l: Soon after another chain came flying up and had the shape of the figure two: then the huntsman bade the other likewise fetch one down from each corner, and to him his trial-shot succeeded also.
sentences.i: Soon after, another skein came flying up in the shape of the figure two; so the huntsman bade the other bring one down from each corner as well, and his trial shot succeeded too.
sentences.n: gelingen takes a dative: the shot succeeds *to him*.

sentences.t: Nun sagte der Pflegevater „ich spreche euch frei, ihr seid ausgelernte Jäger.“
sentences.l: Now the foster-father said “I speak you free, you are fully-trained huntsmen.”
sentences.i: Then the foster father said, “I release you; you are huntsmen now, out of your apprenticeship.”

sentences.t: Darauf giengen die zwei Brüder zusammen in den Wald, rathschlagten mit einander und verabredeten etwas.
sentences.l: Thereupon the two brothers went together into the forest, took counsel with one another and agreed on something.
sentences.n: rathschlagen (modern ratschlagen) = to take counsel, to deliberate together.

sentences.t: Und als sie Abends sich zum Essen niedergesetzt hatten, sagten sie zu ihrem Pflegevater „wir rühren die Speise nicht an, und nehmen keinen Bissen, bevor ihr uns eine Bitte gewährt habt.“
sentences.l: And when in the evening they had sat themselves down to the meal, they said to their foster-father “we do not touch the food, and take no bite, before you have granted us a request.”
sentences.i: And when they had sat down to supper in the evening, they said to their foster father, “We will not touch the food, nor take a bite, until you have granted us a request.”
sentences.n: anrühren = to touch (food). The sons address the old man with the respectful plural ihr.

sentences.t: Sprach er „was ist denn eure Bitte?“
sentences.l: Said he “what then is your request?”
sentences.i: Said he, “And what is your request?”

sentences.t: Sie antworteten „wir haben nun ausgelernt, wir müssen uns auch in der Welt versuchen, so erlaubt daß wir fortziehen und wandern.“
sentences.l: They answered “we have now finished learning, we must also try ourselves in the world, so allow that we move off and wander.”
sentences.i: They answered, “We have served out our time; now we must try ourselves in the world, so permit us to set out and go wandering.”
sentences.n: wandern is the journeyman’s word: the years on the road that follow an apprenticeship.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Alte mit Freuden „ihr redet wie brave Jäger, was ihr begehrt ist mein eigener Wunsch gewesen; zieht aus, es wird euch wohl ergehen.“
sentences.l: Then said the old one with joy “you speak like sound huntsmen, what you desire has been my own wish; set out, it will go well with you.”
sentences.i: Then the old man said joyfully, “You speak like true huntsmen; what you ask has been my own wish. Set out — it will go well with you.”
sentences.n: “es wird euch wohl ergehen” — ergehen is impersonal with a dative, it will fare well *to you*. brav here is upstanding, sound, not “well-behaved.”

sentences.t: Darauf aßen und tranken sie fröhlich zusammen.
sentences.l: Thereupon they ate and drank merrily together.

sentences.t: Als der bestimmte Tag kam, schenkte der Pflegevater jedem eine gute Büchse und einen Hund und ließ jeden von seinen gesparten Goldstücken nehmen so viel er wollte.
sentences.l: When the appointed day came, the foster-father made each a present of a good rifle and a dog and let each take of his saved gold-pieces as much as he wanted.
sentences.i: When the appointed day came, the foster father gave each of them a good rifle and a dog, and let each take as many of his saved gold pieces as he wished.
sentences.n: Büchse is a rifle — a hunting piece, as against the smooth-bore Flinte that turns up later.

sentences.t: Darauf begleitete er sie ein Stück Wegs und beim Abschied gab er ihnen noch ein blankes Messer und sprach „wann ihr euch einmal trennt, so stoßt dies Messer am Scheideweg in einen Baum, daran kann einer, wenn er zurückkommt, sehen wie es seinem abwesenden Bruder ergangen ist, denn die Seite, nach welcher dieser ausgezogen ist, rostet, wann er stirbt: so lange er aber lebt, bleibt sie blank.“
sentences.l: Thereupon he accompanied them a stretch of the way and at the parting gave them besides a bright knife and said “when you one day part, then thrust this knife at the parting-of-the-ways into a tree; by it one of you, when he comes back, can see how it has gone with his absent brother, for the side toward which that one has set out rusts when he dies: but so long as he lives it stays bright.”
sentences.i: Then he went with them a stretch of the road, and at parting gave them besides a bright knife, and said, “When one day you part, thrust this knife into a tree at the crossroads. By it either of you, coming back, may see how it has gone with his absent brother; for the side he set out toward will rust when he dies, but so long as he lives it stays bright.”
sentences.n: The life-token — an object left behind that shows at a distance whether the absent one still lives — is one of the oldest devices in the tales. wann stands here for modern wenn.

sentences.t: Die zwei Brüder giengen immer weiter fort und kamen in einen Wald, so groß, daß sie unmöglich in einem Tag heraus konnten.
sentences.l: The two brothers went ever further away and came into a forest so great that they could not possibly be out of it in one day.
sentences.i: The two brothers went further and further, and came into a forest so vast that they could not possibly get out of it in a single day.
sentences.n: “heraus konnten” — after a modal, German simply drops the verb of motion: could [get] out.

sentences.t: Also blieben sie die Nacht darin und aßen was sie in die Jägertasche gesteckt hatten; sie giengen aber auch noch den zweiten Tag und kamen nicht heraus.
sentences.l: So they stayed the night in it and ate what they had stuck into the hunting-bag; but they walked the second day as well and did not come out.
sentences.i: So they passed the night in it and ate what they had put into their game bags; but they walked a second day too, and still did not come out.
sentences.n: also here is “thus, so,” not English “also.”

sentences.t: Da sie nichts zu essen hatten, so sprach der eine „wir müssen uns etwas schießen, sonst leiden wir Hunger,“ lud seine Büchse und sah sich um.
sentences.l: Since they had nothing to eat, so said the one “we must shoot ourselves something, otherwise we suffer hunger,” loaded his rifle and looked about himself.
sentences.i: Since they had nothing to eat, one of them said, “We must shoot ourselves something, or we shall go hungry,” and he loaded his rifle and looked about him.

sentences.t: Und als ein alter Hase daher gelaufen kam, legte er an, aber der Hase rief
sentences.l: And when an old hare came running along, he took aim, but the hare called
sentences.n: anlegen = to level a gun, to take aim.

sentences.t:
„lieber Jäger, laß mich leben,
ich will dir auch zwei Junge geben.“
sentences.l:
“dear huntsman, let me live,
and two young ones I will give you too.”
sentences.i:
“Dear huntsman, spare my life,
and I will give you two of my young.”
sentences.n: These same two rhymed lines are spoken in turn by hare, fox, wolf, bear and lion — the tale’s bargaining formula, and the reason the brothers end with ten beasts. leben/geben rhymes in German; the English does not chase the rhyme.

sentences.t: Sprang auch gleich ins Gebüsch und brachte zwei Junge; die Thierlein spielten aber so munter und waren so artig, daß die Jäger es nicht übers Herz bringen konnten sie zu tödten.
sentences.l: Sprang also at once into the bushes and brought two young ones; the little-animals played however so merrily and were so well-mannered that the huntsmen could not bring it over their heart to kill them.
sentences.i: And at once it sprang into the bushes and brought two young ones; but the little creatures played so merrily and were so well-behaved that the huntsmen could not find it in their hearts to kill them.
sentences.n: The sentence has no subject of its own — the hare is simply carried over from the verse. “es nicht übers Herz bringen” = not to be able to bring oneself to do a thing.

sentences.t: Sie behielten sie also bei sich, und die kleinen Hasen folgten ihnen auf dem Fuße nach.
sentences.l: So they kept them by them, and the little hares followed after them on the foot.
sentences.i: So they kept them by them, and the little hares followed close at their heels.
sentences.n: “auf dem Fuße nachfolgen” = to follow at someone’s heels.

sentences.t: Bald darauf schlich ein Fuchs vorbei, den wollten sie niederschießen, aber der Fuchs rief
sentences.l: Soon after a fox slunk past; him they wanted to shoot down, but the fox called

sentences.t:
„lieber Jäger, laß mich leben,
ich will dir auch zwei Junge geben.“
sentences.l:
“dear huntsman, let me live,
and two young ones I will give you too.”
sentences.i:
“Dear huntsman, spare my life,
and I will give you two of my young.”

sentences.t: Er brachte auch zwei Füchslein, und die Jäger mochten sie auch nicht tödten, gaben sie den Hasen zur Gesellschaft, und sie folgten ihnen nach.
sentences.l: He brought two little-foxes too, and the huntsmen did not care to kill these either, gave them to the hares for company, and they followed after them.
sentences.i: He too brought two little foxes, and the huntsmen had no wish to kill these either; they gave them to the hares for company, and they followed after.
sentences.n: mögen here carries its older sense, to want or care to.

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so schritt ein Wolf aus dem Dickicht, die Jäger legten auf ihn an, aber der Wolf rief
sentences.l: Not long, and a wolf strode out of the thicket; the huntsmen took aim at him, but the wolf called
sentences.i: It was not long before a wolf strode out of the thicket; the huntsmen took aim at him, but the wolf called
sentences.n: “nicht lange, so …” = it was not long before …

sentences.t:
„lieber Jäger, laß mich leben,
ich will dir auch zwei Junge geben.“
sentences.l:
“dear huntsman, let me live,
and two young ones I will give you too.”
sentences.i:
“Dear huntsman, spare my life,
and I will give you two of my young.”

sentences.t: Die zwei jungen Wölfe thaten die Jäger zu den andern Thieren, und sie folgten ihnen nach.
sentences.l: The two young wolves the huntsmen put with the other animals, and they followed after them.
sentences.i: The huntsmen put the two young wolves with the rest of the animals, and they followed after.

sentences.t: Darauf kam ein Bär, der wollte gern noch länger herumtraben, und rief
sentences.l: Thereupon came a bear, who wanted gladly to trot about still longer, and called
sentences.i: Thereupon came a bear that would gladly have gone on trotting about a while longer, and it called

sentences.t:
„lieber Jäger, laß mich leben,
ich will dir auch zwei Junge geben.“
sentences.l:
“dear huntsman, let me live,
and two young ones I will give you too.”
sentences.i:
“Dear huntsman, spare my life,
and I will give you two of my young.”

sentences.t: Die zwei jungen Bären wurden zu den andern gesellt, und waren ihrer schon acht.
sentences.l: The two young bears were joined to the others, and there were of them already eight.
sentences.i: The two young bears were added to the rest, and now there were eight of them.
sentences.n: “waren ihrer schon acht” — a partitive genitive: of them there were already eight.

sentences.t: Endlich, wer kam? ein Löwe kam und schüttelte seine Mähnen.
sentences.l: At last, who came? a lion came and shook his manes.
sentences.i: At last — who should come? A lion came, and shook his mane.
sentences.n: The question is the teller’s aside to the listener, not part of the action. Mähnen stands in the plural where English keeps the singular.

sentences.t: Aber die Jäger ließen sich nicht schrecken und zielten auf ihn: aber der Löwe sprach gleichfalls
sentences.l: But the huntsmen did not let themselves be frightened and aimed at him: but the lion spoke likewise
sentences.i: But the huntsmen would not be frightened, and took aim at him; the lion, however, spoke in the same way

sentences.t:
„lieber Jäger, laß mich leben,
ich will dir auch zwei Junge geben.“
sentences.l:
“dear huntsman, let me live,
and two young ones I will give you too.”
sentences.i:
“Dear huntsman, spare my life,
and I will give you two of my young.”

sentences.t: Er holte auch seine Jungen herbei, und nun hatten die Jäger zwei Löwen, zwei Bären, zwei Wölfe, zwei Füchse und zwei Hasen, die ihnen nachzogen und dienten.
sentences.l: He too fetched his young ones over, and now the huntsmen had two lions, two bears, two wolves, two foxes and two hares, which went along after them and served them.
sentences.i: He too fetched his young ones, and now the huntsmen had two lions, two bears, two wolves, two foxes and two hares, which followed after them and served them.

sentences.t: Indessen war ihr Hunger damit nicht gestillt worden, da sprachen sie zu den Füchsen, „hört, ihr Schleicher, schafft uns etwas zu essen, ihr seid ja listig und verschlagen.“
sentences.l: Meanwhile their hunger had not been stilled by all this, so they said to the foxes, “listen, you slinkers, get us something to eat, you are indeed sly and crafty.”
sentences.i: All this while their hunger had not been stilled, so they said to the foxes, “Listen, you skulkers, get us something to eat — you are sly and crafty enough.”
sentences.n: Schleicher, from schleichen (to slink), is a name coined on the spot for the foxes. The little word ja inside the clause appeals to what both sides already know.

sentences.t: Sie antworteten „nicht weit von hier liegt ein Dorf, wo wir schon manches Huhn geholt haben; den Weg dahin wollen wir euch zeigen.“
sentences.l: They answered “not far from here lies a village, where we have already fetched many a hen; the way there we will show you.”
sentences.i: They answered, “Not far from here lies a village where we have fetched many a hen before now; we will show you the way there.”

sentences.t: Da giengen sie ins Dorf, kauften sich etwas zu essen und ließen auch ihren Thieren Futter geben, und zogen dann weiter.
sentences.l: So they went into the village, bought themselves something to eat and had fodder given to their animals too, and then moved on.

sentences.t: Die Füchse aber wußten guten Bescheid in der Gegend, wo die Hühnerhöfe waren und konnten die Jäger überall zurecht weisen.
sentences.l: The foxes however knew their way about well in that country, where the hen-yards were, and could set the huntsmen right everywhere.
sentences.i: But the foxes knew the country well — where the hen-yards lay — and could set the huntsmen right wherever they went.
sentences.n: “Bescheid wissen” = to know one’s way about, to be in the know. “zurecht weisen” here is to direct someone rightly; the modern one-word zurechtweisen has hardened into “to reprimand.”

sentences.t: Nun zogen sie eine Weile herum, konnten aber keinen Dienst finden, wo sie zusammen geblieben wären, da sprachen sie „es geht nicht anders, wir müssen uns trennen.“
sentences.l: Now they moved about a while, but could find no service in which they would have stayed together, so they said “it goes not otherwise, we must part.”
sentences.i: Now they roamed about for a while, but could find no post where they might have stayed together, so they said, “There is no help for it — we must part.”
sentences.n: Dienst is a place in someone’s service, what a trained huntsman goes looking for. “es geht nicht anders” = there is no other way.

sentences.t: Sie theilten die Thiere, so daß jeder einen Löwen, einen Bären, einen Wolf, einen Fuchs und einen Hasen bekam: dann nahmen sie Abschied, versprachen sich brüderliche Liebe bis in den Tod und stießen das Messer, das ihnen ihr Pflegevater mitgegeben, in einen Baum; worauf der eine nach Osten, der andere nach Westen zog.
sentences.l: They divided the animals, so that each got a lion, a bear, a wolf, a fox and a hare: then they took leave, promised one another brotherly love unto death and thrust the knife, which their foster-father had given them along, into a tree; whereupon the one moved toward the east, the other toward the west.
sentences.i: They divided the animals, so that each had a lion, a bear, a wolf, a fox and a hare; then they took leave of one another, promised each other brotherly love unto death, and thrust into a tree the knife their foster father had given them — whereupon the one went east and the other west.
sentences.n: “das ihnen ihr Pflegevater mitgegeben” drops the auxiliary hatte, which the tales do freely in a relative clause.

sentences.t: Der jüngste aber kam mit seinen Thieren in eine Stadt, die war ganz mit schwarzem Flor überzogen.
sentences.l: The youngest however came with his animals into a town, which was entirely covered over with black crape.
sentences.i: But the younger came with his animals to a town that was all hung with black crape.
sentences.n: Flor is the thin black gauze of mourning; a whole town draped in it is a public sign of grief. jüngste is a superlative used of one of only two — the tales are not strict about that.

sentences.t: Er gieng in ein Wirthshaus und fragte den Wirth ob er nicht seine Thiere herbergen könnte.
sentences.l: He went into an inn and asked the innkeeper whether he could not lodge his animals.

sentences.t: Der Wirth gab ihnen einen Stall, wo in der Wand ein Loch war: da kroch der Hase hinaus und holte sich ein Kohlhaupt, und der Fuchs holte sich ein Huhn, und als er das gefressen hatte, auch den Hahn dazu; der Wolf aber, der Bär und der Löwe, weil sie zu groß waren, konnten nicht hinaus.
sentences.l: The innkeeper gave them a stable, where there was a hole in the wall: there the hare crept out and fetched himself a cabbage-head, and the fox fetched himself a hen, and when he had devoured that, the cock along with it; the wolf however, the bear and the lion, because they were too big, could not get out.
sentences.i: The innkeeper gave them a stable with a hole in the wall; out through it the hare crept and fetched himself a head of cabbage, and the fox fetched himself a hen, and when he had eaten that, the cock as well. But the wolf, the bear and the lion were too big and could not get out.
sentences.n: fressen is the verb for a beast feeding, essen for a person.

sentences.t: Da ließ sie der Wirth hinbringen, wo eben eine Kuh auf dem Rasen lag, daß sie sich satt fraßen.
sentences.l: Then the innkeeper had them taken to where a cow just then lay on the grass, so that they ate themselves full.
sentences.i: So the innkeeper had them taken to a place where a cow happened to be lying on the grass, and there they ate their fill.
sentences.n: “sich satt fressen” = to eat oneself full.

sentences.t: Und als der Jäger für seine Thiere gesorgt hatte, fragte er erst den Wirth, warum die Stadt so mit Trauerflor ausgehängt wäre?
sentences.l: And when the huntsman had provided for his animals, only then did he ask the innkeeper why the town was so hung out with mourning-crape.
sentences.i: And when the huntsman had seen to his animals, then he asked the innkeeper why the town was hung out with mourning crape.
sentences.n: erst here = only then, not before. The question mark stands although the question is reported — the 1857 text punctuates by the sound of the words.

sentences.t: Sprach der Wirth „weil morgen unseres Königs einzige Tochter sterben wird.“
sentences.l: Said the innkeeper “because to-morrow our king’s only daughter will die.”

sentences.t: Fragte der Jäger „ist sie sterbenskrank?“
sentences.l: Asked the huntsman “is she sick unto death?”
sentences.n: sterbenskrank — ill to the point of dying.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete der Wirth, „sie ist frisch und gesund, aber sie muß doch sterben.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered the innkeeper, “she is fresh and healthy, but she must die all the same.”
sentences.i: “No,” answered the innkeeper, “she is hale and well, and yet she must die.”

sentences.t: „Wie geht das zu?“ fragte der Jäger.
sentences.l: “How does that come about?” asked the huntsman.

sentences.t: „Draußen vor der Stadt ist ein hoher Berg, darauf wohnt ein Drache, der muß alle Jahr eine reine Jungfrau haben, sonst verwüstet er das ganze Land. Nun sind schon alle Jungfrauen hingegeben, und ist niemand mehr übrig, als die Königstochter, dennoch ist keine Gnade, sie muß ihm überliefert werden; und das soll morgen geschehen.“
sentences.l: “Outside before the town there is a high mountain, on it dwells a dragon, who must have a pure maiden every year, otherwise he lays waste the whole land. Now all the maidens have already been given over, and there is no one left but the king’s daughter; even so there is no mercy, she must be delivered up to him; and that is to happen to-morrow.”
sentences.i: “Outside the town there is a high mountain, and on it dwells a dragon who must have a pure maiden every year, or else he lays the whole land waste. By now all the maidens have been given up, and none is left but the king’s daughter; yet there is no mercy for her — she must be delivered to him, and that is to happen tomorrow.”
sentences.n: A yearly tribute of a maiden to a dragon is the old Andromeda story told again. “alle Jahr” is the older way of saying every year.

sentences.t: Sprach der Jäger „warum wird der Drache nicht getödtet?“
sentences.l: Said the huntsman “why is the dragon not killed?”

sentences.t: „Ach,“ antwortete der Wirth, „so viele Ritter habens versucht, aber allesammt ihr Leben eingebüßt; der König hat dem, der den Drachen besiegt, seine Tochter zur Frau versprochen, und er soll auch nach seinem Tode das Reich erben.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” answered the innkeeper, “so many knights have tried it, but all of them forfeited their lives; the king has promised his daughter to wife to him who conquers the dragon, and he shall also inherit the kingdom after his death.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” answered the innkeeper, “so many knights have tried it, and every one of them forfeited his life. The king has promised his daughter in marriage to whoever overcomes the dragon, and after his own death the man shall inherit the kingdom too.”
sentences.n: einbüßen = to forfeit. “seine Tochter zur Frau versprechen” — German marks the role with zu: promised her *as* a wife.

sentences.t: Der Jäger sagte dazu weiter nichts, aber am andern Morgen nahm er seine Thiere und stieg mit ihnen auf den Drachenberg.
sentences.l: The huntsman said nothing further to that, but the next morning he took his animals and climbed with them up the dragon-mountain.

sentences.t: Da stand oben eine kleine Kirche, und auf dem Altar standen drei gefüllte Becher und dabei war die Schrift „wer die Becher austrinkt, wird der stärkste Mann auf Erden, und wird das Schwert führen, das vor der Thürschwelle vergraben liegt.“
sentences.l: There stood above a little church, and on the altar stood three filled cups, and by them was the writing “whoever drinks the cups out will become the strongest man on earth, and will wield the sword that lies buried before the door-sill.”
sentences.i: At the top stood a little church, and on the altar stood three filled cups, and beside them this inscription: “Whoever drinks the cups dry will become the strongest man on earth, and will wield the sword that lies buried before the threshold.”
sentences.n: Schrift here is the inscription itself. führen with a weapon = to wield.

sentences.t: Der Jäger trank da nicht, gieng hinaus und suchte das Schwert in der Erde, vermochte aber nicht es von der Stelle zu bewegen.
sentences.l: The huntsman did not drink then, went out and sought the sword in the earth, but was not able to move it from the spot.
sentences.i: The huntsman did not drink then; he went out and searched for the sword in the earth, but could not stir it from the spot.
sentences.n: vermögen = to be able, a shade more formal than können.

sentences.t: Da ging er hin und trank die Becher aus und war nun stark genug das Schwert aufzunehmen, und seine Hand konnte es ganz leicht führen.
sentences.l: Then he went there and drank the cups out and was now strong enough to take the sword up, and his hand could wield it quite easily.
sentences.i: Then he went and drank the cups dry, and was now strong enough to take up the sword, and his hand could wield it quite easily.
sentences.n: Here the edition prints ging, though elsewhere in this same tale it writes gieng; the 1857 spelling is not perfectly consistent, and we keep whatever the page has.

sentences.t: Als die Stunde kam, wo die Jungfrau dem Drachen sollte ausgeliefert werden, begleitete sie der König, der Marschall und die Hofleute hinaus.
sentences.l: When the hour came in which the maiden was to be delivered up to the dragon, the king, the marshal and the court-folk accompanied her out.
sentences.n: der Marschall is the marshal of the court, a high officer of the royal household — and the man who will shortly betray her.

sentences.t: Sie sah von weitem den Jäger oben auf dem Drachenberg und meinte der Drache stände da und erwartete sie, und wollte nicht hinaufgehen, endlich aber, weil die ganze Stadt sonst wäre verloren gewesen, mußte sie den schweren Gang thun.
sentences.l: She saw from afar the huntsman above on the dragon-mountain and thought the dragon stood there and was awaiting her, and did not want to go up; at last however, because the whole town would otherwise have been lost, she had to do the heavy walk.
sentences.i: From afar she saw the huntsman up on the dragon mountain, and thought the dragon stood there waiting for her, and she would not go up; but at last, since otherwise the whole town would have been lost, she had to take that heavy walk.
sentences.n: “den schweren Gang thun” — to go the hard road, said of a walk one dreads making.

sentences.t: Der König und die Hofleute kehrten voll großer Trauer heim, des Königs Marschall aber sollte stehen bleiben und aus der Ferne alles mit ansehen.
sentences.l: The king and the court-folk turned home full of great sorrow, the king’s marshal however was to stay standing and look on at everything from a distance.
sentences.i: The king and the court turned home in deep grief, but the king’s marshal was to stay behind and watch it all from a distance.
sentences.n: “mit ansehen” = to look on at a thing, to be witness to it.

sentences.t: Als die Königstochter oben auf den Berg kam, stand da nicht der Drache, sondern der junge Jäger, der sprach ihr Trost ein und sagte er wollte sie retten, führte sie in die Kirche und verschloß sie darin.
sentences.l: When the king’s daughter came up onto the mountain, there stood not the dragon but the young huntsman, who spoke comfort into her and said he would save her, led her into the church and locked her in it.
sentences.i: When the king’s daughter came up the mountain, it was not the dragon standing there but the young huntsman; he spoke comfort to her and said he would save her, led her into the church and locked her in.
sentences.n: “jemandem Trost einsprechen” — to speak comfort into someone, an old turn for consoling.

sentences.t: Gar nicht lange, so kam mit großem Gebraus der siebenköpfige Drache daher gefahren.
sentences.l: Not long at all, and the seven-headed dragon came rushing along with a great roaring.
sentences.n: fahren keeps here its old sense of rushing or sweeping along, not travelling; Gebraus is the roar such a motion makes.

sentences.t: Als er den Jäger erblickte, verwunderte er sich und sprach „was hast du hier auf dem Berge zu schaffen?“
sentences.l: When he caught sight of the huntsman he was astonished and said “what have you here on the mountain to do?”
sentences.i: When he caught sight of the huntsman he was astonished, and said, “What business have you here on the mountain?”
sentences.n: “zu schaffen haben” = to have business with a thing.

sentences.t: Der Jäger antwortete „ich will mit dir kämpfen.“
sentences.l: The huntsman answered “I will fight with you.”

sentences.t: Sprach der Drache „so mancher Rittersmann hat hier sein Leben gelassen, mit dir will ich auch fertig werden,“ und athmete Feuer aus sieben Rachen.
sentences.l: Said the dragon “so many a knight has left his life here, with you too I shall get finished,” and breathed fire out of seven maws.
sentences.i: Said the dragon, “Many a knight has left his life here; I shall make an end of you too” — and he breathed fire out of seven throats.
sentences.n: “sein Leben lassen” = to lose one’s life. “mit jemandem fertig werden” = to get the better of him, to finish him. Rachen is a beast’s gaping throat.

sentences.t: Das Feuer sollte das trockne Gras anzünden und der Jäger sollte in der Glut und dem Dampf ersticken, aber die Thiere kamen herbeigelaufen und traten das Feuer aus.
sentences.l: The fire was to kindle the dry grass and the huntsman was to choke in the heat and the smoke, but the animals came running up and trod the fire out.
sentences.i: The fire was meant to kindle the dry grass and the huntsman to choke in the heat and the smoke; but the animals came running up and trod the fire out.
sentences.n: sollte here reports the dragon’s intention: it was meant to.

sentences.t: Da fuhr der Drache gegen den Jäger, aber er schwang sein Schwert, daß es in der Luft sang, und schlug ihm drei Köpfe ab.
sentences.l: Then the dragon rushed against the huntsman, but he swung his sword so that it sang in the air, and struck three heads off him.
sentences.i: Then the dragon rushed at the huntsman; but he swung his sword till it sang in the air, and struck off three of his heads.

sentences.t: Da ward der Drache erst recht wüthend, erhob sich in die Luft, spie die Feuerflammen über den Jäger aus und wollte sich auf ihn stürzen, aber der Jäger zückte nochmals sein Schwert und hieb ihm wieder drei Köpfe ab.
sentences.l: Then the dragon grew only the more furious, raised himself into the air, spewed the fire-flames out over the huntsman and wanted to hurl himself upon him, but the huntsman drew his sword once more and hewed three more heads off him.
sentences.i: At that the dragon grew angrier still, rose into the air, spewed his flames of fire over the huntsman and made to hurl himself upon him; but the huntsman drew his sword again and hewed off three more heads.
sentences.n: “erst recht” = all the more, more than ever.

sentences.t: Das Unthier ward matt und sank nieder, und wollte doch wieder auf den Jäger los, aber er schlug ihm mit der letzten Kraft den Schweif ab, und weil er nicht mehr kämpfen konnte, rief er seine Thiere herbei, die zerrissen es in Stücke.
sentences.l: The monster grew faint and sank down, and yet wanted at the huntsman again, but he struck its tail off with his last strength, and because he could fight no more, he called his animals over, and they tore it into pieces.
sentences.i: The monster grew faint and sank down, yet it made for the huntsman once more; but with his last strength he struck off its tail, and since he could fight no longer he called his animals up, and they tore it to pieces.
sentences.n: “auf jemanden los wollen” — to want *at* someone; after the modal the verb of motion simply drops out.

sentences.t: Als der Kampf zu Ende war, schloß der Jäger die Kirche auf, und fand die Königstochter auf der Erde liegen, weil ihr die Sinne vor Angst und Schrecken während des Streites vergangen waren.
sentences.l: When the fight was at an end, the huntsman unlocked the church and found the king’s daughter lying on the ground, because her senses had gone from her out of fear and terror during the struggle.
sentences.i: When the fight was over, the huntsman unlocked the church and found the king’s daughter lying on the ground, for her senses had left her out of fear and terror during the struggle.
sentences.n: “die Sinne vergiengen ihr” — the senses passed away from her, the old way of saying she fainted, with the person standing in the dative.

sentences.t: Er trug sie heraus, und als sie wieder zu sich selbst kam und die Augen aufschlug, zeigte er ihr den zerrissenen Drachen und sagte ihr daß sie nun erlöst wäre.
sentences.l: He carried her out, and when she came to herself again and struck her eyes open, he showed her the torn dragon and told her that she was now delivered.
sentences.i: He carried her out, and when she came to herself again and opened her eyes, he showed her the dragon torn to pieces and told her that she was delivered now.
sentences.n: “die Augen aufschlagen” — to strike the eyes open, that is, simply to open them.

sentences.t: Sie freute sich und sprach „nun wirst du mein liebster Gemahl werden, denn mein Vater hat mich demjenigen versprochen, der den Drachen tödtet.“
sentences.l: She rejoiced and said “now you will become my dearest husband, for my father has promised me to that one who kills the dragon.”
sentences.i: She rejoiced and said, “Now you shall be my dearest husband, for my father has promised me to the man who kills the dragon.”

sentences.t: Darauf hieng sie ihr Halsband von Korallen ab, und vertheilte es unter die Thiere, um sie zu belohnen, und der Löwe erhielt das goldene Schlößchen davon.
sentences.l: Thereupon she took off her necklace of corals and divided it among the animals, in order to reward them, and the lion received the little golden clasp of it.
sentences.i: Thereupon she took off her coral necklace and divided it among the animals to reward them, and the lion received its little golden clasp.
sentences.n: Schloß is both a lock or clasp and a castle; the diminutive Schlößchen here is the necklace’s golden catch, and it is what will identify the true bridegroom at the end.

sentences.t: Ihr Taschentuch aber, in dem ihr Name stand, schenkte sie dem Jäger, der gieng hin und schnitt aus den sieben Drachenköpfen die Zungen aus, wickelte sie in das Tuch und verwahrte sie wohl.
sentences.l: Her handkerchief however, in which her name stood, she gave to the huntsman; he went and cut the tongues out of the seven dragon-heads, wrapped them in the cloth and kept them well.
sentences.i: But her handkerchief, with her name worked into it, she gave to the huntsman; and he went and cut the tongues out of the seven dragon heads, wrapped them in the cloth and put them safely by.
sentences.n: The tongues are the proof of the true slayer: heads can be carried off by anyone who comes upon the carcass, the tongues only by the man who was there first.

sentences.t: Als das geschehen war, weil er von dem Feuer und dem Kampf so matt und müde war, sprach er zur Jungfrau „wir sind beide so matt und müde, wir wollen ein wenig schlafen.“
sentences.l: When that had happened, because he was so faint and weary from the fire and the fight, he said to the maiden “we are both so faint and weary, we will sleep a little.”
sentences.i: When that was done, being so faint and weary from the fire and the fight, he said to the maiden, “We are both so faint and weary; let us sleep a little.”

sentences.t: Da sagte sie ja, und sie ließen sich auf die Erde nieder, und der Jäger sprach zu dem Löwen „du sollst wachen, damit uns niemand im Schlaf überfällt,“ und beide schliefen ein.
sentences.l: Then she said yes, and they let themselves down onto the ground, and the huntsman said to the lion “you shall keep watch, so that no one falls upon us in our sleep,” and both fell asleep.
sentences.n: “sich niederlassen” = to let oneself down, to settle down.

sentences.t: Der Löwe legte sich neben sie um zu wachen, aber er war vom Kampf auch müde, daß er den Bären rief und sprach „lege dich neben mich, ich muß ein wenig schlafen, und wenn was kommt so wecke mich auf.“
sentences.l: The lion laid himself beside them in order to keep watch, but he too was weary from the fight, so that he called the bear and said “lay yourself beside me, I must sleep a little, and if anything comes, then wake me up.”
sentences.i: The lion lay down beside them to keep watch, but he too was weary from the fight, so that he called the bear and said, “Lie down beside me; I must sleep a little, and if anything comes, wake me.”
sentences.n: The same words now travel down the whole line of beasts, each passing the watch to the next; the dread is built out of exact repetition. was is the everyday short form of etwas.

sentences.t: Da legte sich der Bär neben ihn, aber er war auch müde und rief den Wolf und sprach „lege dich neben mich, ich muß ein wenig schlafen, und wenn was kommt, so wecke mich auf.“
sentences.l: Then the bear laid himself beside him, but he too was weary and called the wolf and said “lay yourself beside me, I must sleep a little, and if anything comes, then wake me up.”
sentences.i: Then the bear lay down beside him, but he too was weary, and called the wolf and said, “Lie down beside me; I must sleep a little, and if anything comes, wake me.”

sentences.t: Da legte sich der Wolf neben ihn, aber er war auch müde und rief den Fuchs und sprach „lege dich neben mich, ich muß ein wenig schlafen, und wenn was kommt, so wecke mich auf.“
sentences.l: Then the wolf laid himself beside him, but he too was weary and called the fox and said “lay yourself beside me, I must sleep a little, and if anything comes, then wake me up.”
sentences.i: Then the wolf lay down beside him, but he too was weary, and called the fox and said, “Lie down beside me; I must sleep a little, and if anything comes, wake me.”

sentences.t: Da legte sich der Fuchs neben ihn, aber er war auch müde, rief den Hasen und sprach „lege dich neben mich, ich muß ein wenig schlafen, und wenn was kommt, so wecke mich auf.“
sentences.l: Then the fox laid himself beside him, but he too was weary and called the hare and said “lay yourself beside me, I must sleep a little, and if anything comes, then wake me up.”
sentences.i: Then the fox lay down beside him, but he too was weary, and called the hare and said, “Lie down beside me; I must sleep a little, and if anything comes, wake me.”

sentences.t: Da setzte sich der Hase neben ihn, aber der arme Has war auch müde, und hatte niemand, den er zur Wache herbeirufen konnte, und schlief ein.
sentences.l: Then the hare set himself beside him, but the poor hare was weary too, and had no one whom he could call over to the watch, and fell asleep.
sentences.n: Has is the short form of Hase.

sentences.t: Da schlief nun die Königstochter, der Jäger, der Löwe, der Bär, der Wolf, der Fuchs und der Has, und schliefen alle einen festen Schlaf.
sentences.l: So now the king’s daughter slept, the huntsman, the lion, the bear, the wolf, the fox and the hare, and they all slept a sound sleep.
sentences.i: And so the king’s daughter slept, and the huntsman, the lion, the bear, the wolf, the fox and the hare, and all of them slept a sound sleep.
sentences.n: “einen festen Schlaf schlafen” — a cognate object, as English says to sleep a sound sleep.

sentences.t: Der Marschall aber, der von weitem hatte zuschauen sollen, als er den Drachen nicht mit der Jungfrau fortfliegen sah, und alles auf dem Berg ruhig ward, nahm sich ein Herz und stieg hinauf.
sentences.l: The marshal however, who was to have looked on from afar, when he did not see the dragon fly off with the maiden, and everything on the mountain grew quiet, took himself a heart and climbed up.
sentences.i: But the marshal, who was to have watched from afar, seeing that the dragon did not fly off with the maiden, and that all grew quiet on the mountain, took heart and climbed up.
sentences.n: “sich ein Herz nehmen” = to take heart, to summon one’s courage.

sentences.t: Da lag der Drache zerstückt und zerrissen auf der Erde und nicht weit davon die Königstochter und ein Jäger mit seinen Thieren, die waren alle in tiefen Schlaf versunken.
sentences.l: There lay the dragon hacked in pieces and torn on the ground, and not far from it the king’s daughter and a huntsman with his animals, who were all sunk in deep sleep.
sentences.i: There lay the dragon on the ground, hacked and torn to pieces, and not far off the king’s daughter and a huntsman with his animals, all of them sunk in deep sleep.

sentences.t: Und weil er bös und gottlos war, so nahm er sein Schwert und hieb dem Jäger das Haupt ab, und faßte die Jungfrau auf den Arm und trug sie den Berg hinab.
sentences.l: And because he was evil and godless, so he took his sword and hewed the head off the huntsman, and took the maiden up on his arm and carried her down the mountain.
sentences.i: And because he was evil and godless, he took his sword and hewed off the huntsman’s head, took the maiden up on his arm and carried her down the mountain.
sentences.n: Haupt is the higher, graver word for head; Kopf is the everyday one, and the tale uses both.

sentences.t: Da erwachte sie und erschrack, aber der Marschall sprach „du bist in meinen Händen, du sollst sagen daß ich es gewesen bin, der den Drachen getödtet hat.“
sentences.l: Then she awoke and was terrified, but the marshal said “you are in my hands, you shall say that it was I who killed the dragon.”
sentences.n: erschrack is the 1857 spelling of erschrak.

sentences.t: „Das kann ich nicht,“ antwortete sie, „denn ein Jäger mit seinen Thieren hats gethan.“
sentences.l: “That I cannot,” she answered, “for a huntsman with his animals has done it.”
sentences.i: “That I cannot do,” she answered, “for it was a huntsman with his animals who did it.”

sentences.t: Da zog er sein Schwert und drohte sie zu tödten, wo sie ihm nicht gehorchte, und zwang sie damit daß sie es versprach.
sentences.l: Then he drew his sword and threatened to kill her if she did not obey him, and forced her by that to promise it.
sentences.n: wo here stands for wenn — an old conditional “if,” not “where.”

sentences.t: Darauf brachte er sie vor den König, der sich vor Freuden nicht zu lassen wußte, als er sein liebes Kind wieder lebend erblickte, das er von dem Unthier zerrissen glaubte.
sentences.l: Thereupon he brought her before the king, who did not know how to contain himself for joy when he caught sight of his dear child alive again, whom he had believed torn to pieces by the monster.
sentences.n: “sich vor Freuden nicht zu lassen wissen” — not to know what to do with oneself for joy.

sentences.t: Der Marschall sprach zu ihm „ich habe den Drachen getödtet, und die Jungfrau und das ganze Reich befreit, darum fordere ich sie zur Gemahlin, so wie es zugesagt ist.“
sentences.l: The marshal said to him “I have killed the dragon and freed the maiden and the whole kingdom; therefore I demand her as wife, just as it was promised.”
sentences.i: The marshal said to him, “I have killed the dragon and freed the maiden and the whole kingdom; therefore I claim her as my wife, just as was promised.”

sentences.t: Der König fragte die Jungfrau „ist das wahr, was er spricht?“
sentences.l: The king asked the maiden “is that true, what he says?”

sentences.t: „Ach ja,“ antwortete sie, „es muß wohl wahr sein: aber ich halte mir aus daß erst über Jahr und Tag die Hochzeit gefeiert wird,“ denn sie dachte in der Zeit etwas von ihrem lieben Jäger zu hören.
sentences.l: “Ah yes,” she answered, “it must indeed be true: but I stipulate for myself that the wedding be celebrated only when a year and a day are out,” for she thought in that time to hear something of her dear huntsman.
sentences.i: “Ah yes,” she answered, “it must be true; but I make this condition, that the wedding be held only when a year and a day are out” — for she thought that in that time she might hear something of her dear huntsman.
sentences.n: “sich etwas aushalten” here is to stipulate, to make a condition for oneself. “Jahr und Tag” is a legal formula for a set waiting period — a year with a customary few days added.

sentences.t: Auf dem Drachenberg aber lagen noch die Thiere neben ihrem todten Herrn und schliefen, da kam eine große Hummel und setzte sich dem Hasen auf die Nase, aber der Hase wischte sie mit der Pfote ab und schlief weiter.
sentences.l: On the dragon-mountain however the animals still lay beside their dead master and slept; then came a great bumble-bee and settled on the hare’s nose, but the hare wiped it off with his paw and slept on.
sentences.i: But on the dragon mountain the animals still lay sleeping beside their dead master; and there came a great bumblebee and settled on the hare’s nose, but the hare wiped it away with his paw and slept on.

sentences.t: Die Hummel kam zum zweitenmal, aber der Hase wischte sie wieder ab und schlief fort.
sentences.l: The bumble-bee came a second time, but the hare wiped it off again and slept on.

sentences.t: Da kam sie zum drittenmal und stach ihm in die Nase, daß er aufwachte.
sentences.l: Then it came a third time and stung him in the nose, so that he woke up.

sentences.t: Sobald der Hase wach war, weckte er den Fuchs, und der Fuchs den Wolf, und der Wolf den Bär, und der Bär den Löwen.
sentences.l: As soon as the hare was awake, he woke the fox, and the fox the wolf, and the wolf the bear, and the bear the lion.
sentences.n: The chain of the watch now runs back up the other way. den Bär stands where the standard form would be den Bären.

sentences.t: Und als der Löwe aufwachte und sah daß die Jungfrau fort war und sein Herr todt, fieng er an fürchterlich zu brüllen und rief „wer hat das vollbracht? Bär, warum hast du mich nicht geweckt?“
sentences.l: And when the lion woke up and saw that the maiden was gone and his master dead, he began to roar frightfully and cried “who has accomplished this? Bear, why did you not wake me?”
sentences.i: And when the lion woke and saw that the maiden was gone and his master dead, he began to roar frightfully, and cried, “Who has done this? Bear, why did you not wake me?”
sentences.n: vollbringen is a lofty word for carrying a deed through; the lion turns it on the crime.

sentences.t: Der Bär fragte den Wolf „warum hast du mich nicht geweckt?“ und der Wolf den Fuchs „warum hast du mich nicht geweckt?“ und der Fuchs den Hasen „warum hast du mich nicht geweckt?“
sentences.l: The bear asked the wolf “why did you not wake me?” and the wolf the fox “why did you not wake me?” and the fox the hare “why did you not wake me?”
sentences.n: After the first clause the verb drops out — “und der Wolf den Fuchs [fragte]”; the repetition alone carries it.

sentences.t: Der arme Has wußte allein nichts zu antworten, und die Schuld blieb auf ihm hangen.
sentences.l: The poor hare alone knew nothing to answer, and the blame stayed hanging on him.
sentences.i: The poor hare alone had nothing to answer, and the blame stuck to him.
sentences.n: hangen is the older form of hängen; blame that “stays hanging” on a person is blame he cannot shake off.

sentences.t: Da wollten sie über ihn herfallen, aber er bat und sprach „bringt mich nicht um, ich will unsern Herrn wieder lebendig machen. Ich weiß einen Berg, da wächst eine Wurzel, wer die im Mund hat, der wird von aller Krankheit und allen Wunden geheilt. Aber der Berg liegt zweihundert Stunden von hier.“
sentences.l: Then they wanted to fall upon him, but he begged and said “do not kill me, I will make our master alive again. I know a mountain where a root grows; whoever has it in his mouth is healed of every sickness and all wounds. But the mountain lies two hundred hours from here.”
sentences.i: Then they made to fall on him, but he pleaded and said, “Do not kill me; I will make our master alive again. I know a mountain where a root grows, and whoever holds it in his mouth is healed of every sickness and every wound. But the mountain lies two hundred hours away from here.”
sentences.n: A Stunde is here a measure of distance, not of time — as far as a man walks in an hour. The same reckoning returns at the close of the tale.

sentences.t: Sprach der Löwe „in vier und zwanzig Stunden mußt du hin und her gelaufen sein und die Wurzel mitbringen.“
sentences.l: Said the lion “in four and twenty hours you must have run there and back and bring the root with you.”
sentences.n: Now Stunden are hours of time again: two hundred hours of road against a single day to cover it. The 1857 text writes the numeral out in separate words, “vier und zwanzig.”

sentences.t: Da sprang der Hase fort, und in vier und zwanzig Stunden war er zurück, und brachte die Wurzel mit.
sentences.l: Then the hare sprang away, and in four and twenty hours he was back, and brought the root with him.

sentences.t: Der Löwe setzte dem Jäger den Kopf wieder an, und der Hase steckte ihm die Wurzel in den Mund, alsbald fügte sich alles wieder zusammen, und das Herz schlug und das Leben kehrte zurück.
sentences.l: The lion set the head on the huntsman again, and the hare stuck the root into his mouth; at once everything joined itself together again, and the heart beat and life returned.
sentences.n: ansetzen = to set a thing on, to fit it back in place.

sentences.t: Da erwachte der Jäger und erschrack als er die Jungfrau nicht mehr sah, und dachte „sie ist wohl fortgegangen, während ich schlief, um mich los zu werden.“
sentences.l: Then the huntsman awoke and was terrified when he no longer saw the maiden, and thought “she has gone away, I suppose, while I slept, in order to be rid of me.”
sentences.n: wohl softens the thought into a guess. “jemanden los werden” = to get rid of someone.

sentences.t: Der Löwe hatte in der großen Eile seinem Herrn den Kopf verkehrt aufgesetzt, der aber merkte es nicht bei seinen traurigen Gedanken an die Königstochter: erst zu Mittag, als er etwas essen wollte, da sah er daß ihm der Kopf nach dem Rücken zu stand, konnte es nicht begreifen und fragte die Thiere was ihm im Schlaf widerfahren wäre?
sentences.l: The lion in his great haste had set his master’s head on the wrong way round, but he did not notice it amid his sorrowful thoughts of the king’s daughter: only at midday, when he wanted to eat something, did he see that his head faced toward his back; he could not grasp it and asked the animals what had befallen him in his sleep.
sentences.i: In his great haste the lion had set his master’s head on back to front, but the huntsman did not notice it, so sorrowful were his thoughts of the king’s daughter. Only at midday, when he wanted to eat something, did he see that his head faced his own back; he could not make it out, and asked the animals what had befallen him in his sleep.
sentences.n: verkehrt = the wrong way round. widerfahren = to befall someone, with the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Da erzählte ihm der Löwe daß sie auch alle aus Müdigkeit eingeschlafen wären und beim Erwachen hätten sie ihn todt gefunden mit abgeschlagenem Haupte, der Hase hätte die Lebenswurzel geholt, er aber in der Eil den Kopf verkehrt gehalten; doch wollte er seinen Fehler wieder gut machen.
sentences.l: Then the lion told him that they too had all fallen asleep from weariness, and on waking had found him dead with his head struck off; the hare had fetched the root of life, but he in his haste had held the head the wrong way round; still he would make his fault good again.
sentences.i: Then the lion told him that they too had all fallen asleep from weariness, and on waking had found him dead with his head struck off; the hare had fetched the root of life, but he in his haste had held the head the wrong way round — yet he would put his fault right.
sentences.n: The whole report runs in the subjunctive (wären, hätten, hätte), German’s way of marking words as somebody else’s. “wieder gut machen” = to make good, to put right.

sentences.t: Dann riß er dem Jäger den Kopf wieder ab, drehte ihn herum, und der Hase heilte ihn mit der Wurzel fest.
sentences.l: Then he tore the head off the huntsman again, turned it round, and the hare healed it fast with the root.

sentences.t: Der Jäger aber war traurig, zog in der Welt herum und ließ seine Thiere vor den Leuten tanzen.
sentences.l: The huntsman however was sorrowful, moved about in the world and let his animals dance before the people.
sentences.i: But the huntsman was sorrowful; he wandered about the world and made his animals dance before the people.
sentences.n: Showing trained beasts for coin was the trade of travelling players — the king-to-be is reduced to it.

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß er gerade nach Verlauf eines Jahres wieder in dieselbe Stadt kam, wo er die Königstochter vom Drachen erlöst hatte und die Stadt war diesmal ganz mit rothem Scharlach ausgehängt.
sentences.l: It came to pass that just after the passing of a year he came again into the same town where he had delivered the king’s daughter from the dragon, and the town was this time all hung out with red scarlet.
sentences.i: It came to pass that just at the end of a year he came again to the same town where he had delivered the king’s daughter from the dragon; and this time the town was all hung with red scarlet.
sentences.n: Scharlach is scarlet cloth; the black crape of his first arrival is answered by it.

sentences.t: Da sprach er zum Wirth „was will das sagen? vorm Jahr war die Stadt mit schwarzem Flor überzogen, was soll heute der rothe Scharlach?“
sentences.l: Then he said to the innkeeper “what is that to say? a year ago the town was covered with black crape, what is the red scarlet to mean to-day?”
sentences.i: Then he said to the innkeeper, “What does this mean? A year ago the town was hung with black crape; what is the red scarlet for today?”
sentences.n: “was will das sagen?” = what is that supposed to mean? “vorm Jahr” = a year ago.

sentences.t: Der Wirth antwortete „vorm Jahr sollte unsers Königs Tochter dem Drachen ausgeliefert werden, aber der Marschall hat mit ihm gekämpft und ihn getödtet, und da soll morgen ihre Vermählung gefeiert werden; darum war die Stadt damals mit schwarzem Flor zur Trauer, und ist heute mit rothem Scharlach zur Freude ausgehängt.“
sentences.l: The innkeeper answered “a year ago our king’s daughter was to be delivered up to the dragon, but the marshal fought with him and killed him, and so to-morrow their wedding is to be celebrated; that is why the town was then hung with black crape for mourning, and to-day with red scarlet for joy.”

sentences.t: Am andern Tag, wo die Hochzeit sein sollte, sprach der Jäger um Mittagszeit zum Wirth „glaubt er wohl, Herr Wirth, daß ich heut Brot von des Königs Tisch hier bei ihm essen will?“
sentences.l: The next day, on which the wedding was to be, the huntsman said at midday to the innkeeper “does he believe, Master Innkeeper, that to-day I mean to eat bread from the king’s table here in his house?”
sentences.i: The next day, when the wedding was to be, the huntsman said to the innkeeper at midday, “Do you believe, Master Innkeeper, that today I mean to eat bread from the king’s table here in your house?”
sentences.n: The huntsman speaks to the innkeeper in the third person singular — “glaubt er,” “bei ihm,” and later “sieht er” over and over. This is the old Er-form, once the polite address to a tradesman or an inferior; it sounds lordly and archaic now, and English has nothing for it but “you.” It runs through the whole wager.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sprach der Wirth, „da wollt ich doch noch hundert Goldstücke dran setzen, daß das nicht wahr ist.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” said the innkeeper, “and I would stake a hundred gold pieces on it besides, that that is not true.”
sentences.n: “daran setzen” = to stake on it; wollt = wollte.

sentences.t: Der Jäger nahm die Wette an und setzte einen Beutel mit eben so viel Goldstücken dagegen.
sentences.l: The huntsman took the wager up and set a purse with just as many gold-pieces against it.

sentences.t: Dann rief er den Hasen und sprach „geh hin, lieber Springer, und hol mir von dem Brot, das der König ißt.“
sentences.l: Then he called the hare and said “go there, dear Springer, and fetch me some of the bread that the king eats.”
sentences.n: Springer — “leaper” — is a name made for the hare on the spot, as Schleicher was for the foxes.

sentences.t: Nun war das Häslein das geringste und konnte es keinem andern wieder auftragen, sondern mußte sich selbst auf die Beine machen.
sentences.l: Now the little-hare was the lowest, and could not lay it on any other in turn, but had to get himself on his legs.
sentences.i: Now the little hare was the lowliest, and could not pass the errand on to anyone else, but had to take to his legs himself.
sentences.n: “sich auf die Beine machen” = to set off. The rank among the beasts, settled during the watch, holds for errands too.

sentences.t: „Ei,“ dachte es, „wann ich so allein durch die Straßen springe, da werden die Metzgerhunde hinter mir drein sein.“
sentences.l: “Ei,” thought it, “when I go springing through the streets alone like that, the butchers’ dogs will be after me.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” he thought, “if I go leaping through the streets all alone, the butchers’ dogs will be after me.”
sentences.n: The hare is “es” here, neuter, because he is das Häslein. “hinter einem drein sein” = to be after someone.

sentences.t: Wie es dachte, so geschah es auch, und die Hunde kamen hinter ihm drein und wollten ihm sein gutes Fell flicken.
sentences.l: As it thought, so it also happened, and the dogs came after him and wanted to patch his good coat for him.
sentences.i: As he thought, so it fell out: the dogs came after him and meant to mend his good coat for him.
sentences.n: “jemandem das Fell flicken” — to patch someone’s hide, an old joke for giving him a thrashing.
